title: [2607.01203] GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics

sections.heading: GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics

content.text: This paper studies real-time robust optimal control for uncertain nonlinear systems, where linear time-varying (LTV) approximations make planning tractable but require sound linearization error bounds (LEBs) to guarantee robust constraint satisfaction. We develop tight, differentiable, GPU-parallel LEBs for LTV approximations of nonlinear and neural network (NN) dynamics. For analytic dynamics, we introduce path-based Hessian bounds that are tighter than standard interval methods. For NN dynamics, we derive certified LEBs using NN verifier-generated affine relaxations and local Jacobian corrections. We adapt a GPU-parallel system-level synthesis LTV-based robust control solver to be compatible with these LEBs by extending it to handle right-invertible disturbance matrices and non-zero-centered disturbance sets for tight zonotopic uncertainty propagation. Our method, GPUSLS-LEO, enables online optimization of robust feedback policies that account for linearization error, producing tight, formally verified reachable tubes. On complex nonlinear and NN dynamics up to 168 state dimensions, our method can compute robust control policies on the GPU at rates up to 67 Hz, reducing solve times and conservativeness relative to baselines while preserving formal guarantees and real-time performance.

Safe real-time nonlinear control under uncertainty is essential for the resilient operation of robots, drones, and spacecraft. This motivates methods for solving the robust nonlinear optimal control problem (RNOCP), which seeks a control policy that robustly guarantees constraint satisfaction under worst-case disturbances. In practice, RNOCP solvers typically optimize (1) a nominal trajectory and (2) a stabilizing feedback controller to track it under disturbance. Robust constraint satisfaction is enforced by tightening the nominal constraints using an overapproximation of the closed-loop tracking-error reachable tube, ensuring that the closed-loop dynamics remain in a safe subset of the state and input space. However, exact reachability via error propagation through nonlinear dynamics [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib1), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib2), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib3)] is generally intractable in real time. To address this, [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib5), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7)] approximate the nonlinear dynamics along a nominal trajectory with a linear time-varying (LTV) system and compute reachable sets using the LTV dynamics. System-level synthesis (SLS) [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib8), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)] is one such LTV robust control framework that can be solved in real time over long horizons for high-dimensional systems [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)].

Despite strong performance, LTV-based methods only guarantee robust constraint satisfaction given a bound on the linearization error, which captures the deviation between the true nonlinear dynamics and their LTV approximation. Existing methods often use global bounds [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11)], which yield conservative (loose) reachable tubes. Tighter local bounds around the nominal trajectory are often possible, but must be computed efficiently for real-time planning and informative enough to guide the optimizer toward safe trajectories with minimal linearization error. Thus, the challenge is to develop bounds that are simultaneously (1) tight, (2) real-time computable, and (3) differentiable, so an RNOCP solver can use them to reshape the nominal trajectory and tighten the reachable tubes. As existing methods do not achieve all three, many LTV-based RNOCP solvers must omit linearization error, forgoing formal guarantees for performance [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib12), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib13)].

To close this gap, we propose a family of tight, differentiable linearization error bounds (LEBs) for RNOCP solvers with nonlinear dynamics described by analytic functions and neural networks (NNs), with a GPU-parallel implementation in JAX. To make these LEBs compatible with the real-time SLS solver of [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9)], we extend the solver 1) to accommodate right-invertible disturbance matrices, enabling direct zonotopic propagation of the LEBs while avoiding the conservative overapproximations in [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9)]; and 2) to handle disturbance sets that are not zero-centered. Finally, we show empirically that these bounds enable real-time, GPU-based computation of formally verified RNOCP solutions, with limited conservativeness for systems with up to 168 states and solve times as low as 15 ms. Our contributions are:

* • A set of tight, provably-sound linearization error bounding methods, including path-based interval bounds for analytic systems and NN verifier-based bounds for NN dynamics. * • A novel nonlinear SLS formulation that includes linearization error through tight zonotopic propagation, including treatment of right-invertible disturbance matrices and non-zero-centered disturbance sets, guaranteeing robust constraint satisfaction for the original nonlinear system. * • A GPU-accelerated nonlinear SLS solver, GPUSLS-LEO, that uses a formulation of these linearization bounds in JAX to enable differentiable, GPU-parallel evaluation and gradient-based robust nonlinear optimal control. * • Evaluation on analytic and NN dynamics models, maintaining real-time control rates (up to 67 Hz) for systems up to 168D and problems with ≈2×105\approx 2\times 10^{5} decision variables.

While linearization-free reachability methods exist [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib1), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib2), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib3)], direct error propagation through nonlinear dynamics is generally intractable in real time, especially beyond ≈\approx10 states [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib3), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib1)]. Thus, RNOCP solvers often rely on linearized error propagation for efficiency [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib14), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib13)], but introduce linearization error that is difficult to tightly bound, and is often ignored [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib14), [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib15), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib13), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)], underapproximated via sampling [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)], or handled by assuming access to a linearization bound oracle [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib16), [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib17), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib18), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib19), [20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib20)]. RNOCP solvers that explicitly compute LEBs typically rely on global Lipschitz estimates [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11)] or interval arithmetic [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib5), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib21)]. Interval arithmetic has been used both to compute reachable sets [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib22), [23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib23)] and to support reachability by constructing linear differential inclusion bounds (LDI) for nonlinear dynamics [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib24)]. In particular, [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib25)] uses Jacobian overbounding to obtain tighter LDIs for reachability, but is not used for control design or directly compute LEBs. Computationally, existing linearization bounding methods are offline [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)], slow, or non-differentiable [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7)], limiting their use for planning. To close these gaps, our method uses interval arithmetic and JAX to compute tight differentiable LEBs for direct use in optimal control. Moreover, we also adapt neural-network (NN) verification tools [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib26)] to derive affine bounds on linearization error for NN dynamics.

As LEBs can be slow to compute [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)], they are often generated once offline [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11)] but are loose if we wish to bound error around one trajectory, as in RMPC. Thus, practitioners often omit linearization error, yielding heuristic reachable tubes that trade formal guarantees for performance [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib12)]. To address this, we show that tight, local, GPU-parallel LEBs can be computed online while providing both real-time performance on high-dimensional systems and hard guarantees.

children.heading: V-B Efficient SLS Implementation on the GPU

content.text: We propose GPUSLS-Linearization Error Optimization (GPUSLS-LEO), which builds on GPUSLS [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)] to explicitly account for linearization error propagation. We first replace the ellipsoidal disturbance representation of [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)] with a zonotope, modifying the constraint tightenings and cost terms via ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E29 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics"))-([31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E31 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). At each controller update, we modify GPUSLS by including a zonotopic bound on the linearization error via ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E25 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). We then modify the initialization of 𝚽x\mathbf{\Phi}^{\text{x}} via ([34c](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E34.3 "In 34 ‣ V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")).

All other steps closely follow the GPUSLS procedure. In particular, GPUSLS-LEO solves ([24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E24 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) iteratively via sequential quadratic programming (SQP). At each iteration, GPUSLS-LEO quadraticizes the cost and linearizes xk+1=f⁡(xk,uk)x\_{k+1}=f(x\_{k},u\_{k}) around the current (z,v)(\textbf{z},\textbf{v}) to obtain Ak,BkA\_{k},B\_{k} ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S3.E4 "In III-A System Level Synthesis (SLS) ‣ III Preliminaries and Problem Statement ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). It then solves (A) a local QP approximation of ([32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E32 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) to update (z,v)(\textbf{z},\textbf{v}), (B) ([34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E34 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) to get 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi}, and updates (C) the tightenings via ([24f](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E24.6 "In 24 ‣ V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). Since our LEBs are differentiable, we can penalize error accumulation during step (A) by modifying the nominal objective ([32a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E32.1 "In 32 ‣ V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) to J¯​(z,v):=J⁡(z,v)+λ​Jerr​(z,v)\bar{J}(\textbf{z},\textbf{v}):=J(\textbf{z},\textbf{v})+\lambda J\_{\textrm{err}}(\textbf{z},\textbf{v}), where

penalizes the propagated residual error ([8a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S3.E8.1 "In 8 ‣ III-A System Level Synthesis (SLS) ‣ III Preliminaries and Problem Statement ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). Here, 𝚽,𝝁j,𝝈j\mathbf{\Phi},\bm{\mu}\_{j},\bm{\sigma}\_{j} are from the previous iteration and λ\lambda is a weighting term. Notably, ([35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E35 "In V-B Efficient SLS Implementation on the GPU ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) biases (z,v)(\textbf{z},\textbf{v}) toward regions of low propagated exogenous and linearization error disturbances. Finally, we show that by solving ([24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E24 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")), GPUSLS-LEO ensures containment in the reachable tubes ([26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E26 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")), i.e., xk∈Ω¯kxx\_{k}\in\bar{\Omega}\_{k}^{x} and uk∈Ω¯kuu\_{k}\in\bar{\Omega}\_{k}^{u}, for all k∈[N]k\in[N]. Formally, we have (proof in App. [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#A4 "Appendix D Proofs ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")):

Let 𝐳\mathbf{z}, 𝐯\mathbf{v}, and 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} be a feasible solution for ([24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E24 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). Then, ([26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E26 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) is guaranteed to overapproximate the true closed-loop reachable set ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S3.E3 "In III Preliminaries and Problem Statement ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")), i.e., Ωk⊆Ω¯k\Omega\_{k}\subseteq\bar{\Omega}\_{k} for all k∈[N]k\in[N].

We evaluate LEB tightness (Sec. [VI-A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.SS1 "VI-A Linearization Error ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) and the robust controllers given by GPUSLS-LEO (Sec. [VI-B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.SS2 "VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). Runtime tests use an NVIDIA RTX 4090, except the multi-quadrotor and long-horizon experiments, which require an NVIDIA H200. System definitions appear in App. [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#A1 "Appendix A Dynamical System Definitions ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics").

We compare the LEB from our path-based Hessian (PBH) method on the Satellite (nx=7n\_{x}=7, nu=3n\_{u}=3) and Quadrotor (nx=12n\_{x}=12, nu=4n\_{u}=4) systems (App. [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#A1 "Appendix A Dynamical System Definitions ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) with several baselines. Global sampling [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)] estimates worst-case curvature offline (taking over 7 minutes [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)]) over the *global* set 𝒳×𝒰\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}, yielding an empirical over-approximation. Interval Hessian (IH) (classic) [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7)] evaluates ([12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S4.E12 "In IV-A Linearization Error Bounds for Analytic Dynamics ‣ IV GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) on a local set 𝒯⊂(𝒳×𝒰)\mathcal{T}\subset(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}). IH (classic)-CORA denotes the standard IH implementation in CORA [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib29)]. Random sampling uses 10K samples from the local set and gives an *under-approximation*. We sample nominal points (z,v)(z,v) from 𝒳×𝒰\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U} and define local sets 𝒯:=(z,v)⊕ϵ​ℰnx+nu\mathcal{T}:=(z,v)\oplus\epsilon\mathcal{E}\_{n\_{x}+n\_{u}} with ϵ=0.01,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2\epsilon=0.01,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2. Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ VI-A Linearization Error ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") shows the mean interval width of ([23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S4.E23 "In IV-C Zonotope Bounds of ⁢ r k ( x k , u k , w k ) ‣ IV GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). For *Satellite*, where nonlinearity is mild, all over-approximation methods remain close to the random-sampling lower bound as ϵ\epsilon grows, though PBH is still the tightest. For *Quadrotor*, PBH consistently gives the tightest bounds. By contrast, global sampling is loose at small ϵ\epsilon, suggesting global curvature misses local behavior, while the interval Hessian becomes overly conservative at ϵ=0.20\epsilon=0.20. Table [I](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.T1 "TABLE I ‣ VI-A Linearization Error ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") compares online runtime. PBH runs in under 1 ms, enabling real-time use. Although slower than the global bound, which is efficiently calculated online after slow offline computation, PBH is 60% and 27% (satellite and quadrotor respectively) faster than dense random sampling and negligible running time compared to CORA IH.

To quantify the benefit of differentiability in our path-based Hessian implementation, we search for a nominal point within a fixed perturbation radius ϵ\epsilon that minimizes the LEB size. Starting from random nominal points, we run projected gradient descent (PGD) within a local neighborhood of radius ϵopt\epsilon\_{\text{opt}} to reduce the error interval width. We compare PGD with random sampling of nominal points under the same time budget, where both methods use the PBH to evaluate linearization error. Table [II](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.T2 "TABLE II ‣ VI-A Linearization Error ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") shows that across 100% of test cases, PGD yields smaller error interval widths than random sampling across both systems, showing the value of gradient-based optimization for finding nominal points with tighter LEBs, which can benefit downstream SLS.

children.heading: VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP

content.text: In this section, we evaluate GPUSLS-LEO on a suite of analytic and neural dynamical systems against various RNOCP baselines. We further assess the impact of key ablations, including the effect of optimizing over the linearization error gradients and the use of nonzero-centered zonotopes. All benchmarked methods are evaluated under the same disturbance set for the given dynamical system and, where applicable, are run for a maximum of 100 SQP iterations.

We evaluate our method on a 7D satellite attitude control task, where the objective is to stabilize the system to a desired orientation under bounded disturbances. We adopt the experimental setup of [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)] and benchmark against their approach. In Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") (a) we compare the tube widths 𝝈k\bm{\sigma}\_{k} for: GPUSLS-LEO, GPUSLS-E (ellipsoidal propagation as in [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9), App. A]), GPUSLS (no linearization error propagation) [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)], and NL-SLS ( [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)]). Our method achieves the tightest tubes among all baselines. We have on average 20% smaller tubes than NL-SLS, which relies on a global maximum Hessian bound and is therefore locally overly-conservative along a trajectory. Compared to GPUSLS-E, our method achieves 45% smaller tubes, as it involves overapproximating the Minkowski sum of ellipsoids, whereas our zonotope-based combination is exact. We observe that incorporating our LEB pipeline does not introduce significant conservativeness, as the tube widths increase by only 4% compared to GPUSLS. In Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") (b), we show the rollouts of 20 random and 64 adversarial disturbances for the quaternion states, showing 100% containment under our method.

We evaluate our method on a 6D planar quadrotor against control contraction metrics (CCM) [[30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib30)]. Both methods must navigate through a dense obstacle field over a horizon of 40 steps. Fig. [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ VI-B1 Satellite ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a) shows our method achieving 91% smaller tube area than the CCM for the (x,y)(x,y) position states. This arises because the CCM certifies safety over the entire state space, introducing inherent conservativeness. GPUSLS-LEO, on the other hand, certifies safety along a specific trajectory, enabling tighter, trajectory-dependent bounds. We also evaluate the closed-loop system on an interval-based reachability analysis tool immrax [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib24)], showing its calculated tube area diverging after a few steps.

In Fig. [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ VI-B1 Satellite ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(b) we compare the calculated trajectories and tubes for our method and CCM. Our approach is less conservative, allowing a more direct, task-optimal path, while the CCM is forced to take a longer route. In Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ VI-B1 Satellite ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a), we show the trajectory and tubes over a long horizon of 7500 steps, which involves optimizing a state-control trajectory with 1.95×1051.95\times 10^{5} decision variables. Due to the tightness of our LEBs and the optimization of the closed-loop controller in SLS, our tubes remain well-bounded and finite over the horizon (Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ VI-B1 Satellite ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(b)), demonstrating its scalability to long horizons.

To demonstrate scalability to high dimensional systems, we evaluate our method on a coupled system of 14 3D quadrotors (168D) over a horizon of 25. The system is tasked with navigating through an obstacle field while the quadrotors are coupled via a spring force toward the group centroid. We show the planned trajectories and the tubes in Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ VI-B2 Planar quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a), and observe all rollouts remain in the tight tubes despite the high dimensional state space, demonstrating the method’s scalability to state dimensionality. In Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ VI-B2 Planar quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(b), we plot the tubes and the corresponding rollouts for pyp\_{y} and vyv\_{y} for 100 adversarial disturbances.

We demonstrate that our formulation can account for linearization error propagation through learned neural dynamics. We train an MLP-based model for the T-pusher system and task it with rotating and pushing the object to the goal configuration (Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). We evaluate our method on several ablations (Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a)), including GPUSLS, GSL (shorthand for GPUSLS-LEO), GSL-C (zero-centered zonotopes) and GSL (λ=1\lambda=1), which incorporates a penalty on the linearization error as defined in [V-B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.SS2 "V-B Efficient SLS Implementation on the GPU ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics"). Compared to GPUSLS, GPUSLS-LEO produces tubes that are on average 99% larger. However, Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(b) shows that our method achieves 100% containment of all rollouts, while Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(c) illustrates how trajectories from GPUSLS fall out of the tube, showing the need to formally consider linearization error.

Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a) shows that adding linearization error penalties can reduce conservativeness, with λ=1\lambda=1 decreasing tube widths by 8%. We also show the importance of nonzero-centered zonotopes, as using zero-centered zonotopes leads to 25% larger tubes. We present rollouts and disturbance deviations in Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a). In Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(b), we demonstrate the method’s ability for closed-loop MPC on simulated contact dynamics, where the pusher successfully completes the task. We note that we do not formally consider learning error; however, it can be incorporated as in [[31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib31), [32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib32)].

We evaluate the runtime of our method across all systems. In Tab. [III](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.T3 "TABLE III ‣ VI-B4 Neural T-pusher ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics"), we show the per iteration breakdown in milliseconds of the different components of our methodology. In all systems aside from the coupled quadrotor, the main computation load is in the GPUSLS, showing that our proposed modifications do not drastically increase run time. We also show that all total runtimes fall below the discretization time step DT, demonstrating the viability of our method under a real-time iteration MPC scheme [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)].

Finally, we evaluate the method’s scaling with growing state and control dimensions using an increasing number of coupled quadrotors. Fig. [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B4 Neural T-pusher ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") shows that GPUSLS incurs higher initial runtime but scales favorably with state and control dimension due to its logarithmic scaling [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)]. PBH on the other hand, exhibits low initial runtime, but can slow down in higher dimensions due to the cost of Hessian computations.

This paper presents a framework for computing tight, differentiable, and sound linearization error bounds (LEBs) for nonlinear analytic and NN dynamics and for using them in GPUSLS-LEO, a real-time GPU-parallel RNOCP solver based on SLS. The approach reduces conservativeness, outperforming state-of-the-art reachability analysis tools, while maintaining formal guarantees and achieving performance on systems with up to 168 states, real-time control rates (up to 67 Hz), and problems with ≈2×105\approx 2\times 10^{5} decision variables. Future work will investigate how our LEBs can be extended to bound linearization errors for contact-rich planning [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib28)] and nonlinear output-feedback control, including through extensions of the SLS-based methods described in [[33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib33), [34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib34), [35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib35)].

content.text: Solving ([33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E33 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) yields optimal values for 𝚽x\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}} and 𝚽u\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{u}} which penalize the size of the tightenings ([31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E31 "In V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). However, this leads to terms in ([33a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E33.1 "In 33 ‣ V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) that scale the response matrices 𝚽x\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{x}} and 𝚽u\mathbf{\Phi}^{\mathrm{u}} by E¯j\bar{E}\_{j} in the cost ([33a](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.E33.1 "In 33 ‣ V-A Nonlinear SLS Formulation ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). This remains a quadratic cost in 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} but no longer maintains the structure of an LQR cost function. Abstract
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

This paper studies real-time robust optimal control for uncertain nonlinear systems, where linear time-varying (LTV) approximations make planning tractable but require sound linearization error bounds (LEBs) to guarantee robust constraint satisfaction. We develop tight, differentiable, GPU-parallel LEBs for LTV approximations of nonlinear and neural network (NN) dynamics. For analytic dynamics, we introduce path-based Hessian bounds that are tighter than standard interval methods. For NN dynamics, we derive certified LEBs using NN verifier-generated affine relaxations and local Jacobian corrections. We adapt a GPU-parallel system-level synthesis LTV-based robust control solver to be compatible with these LEBs by extending it to handle right-invertible disturbance matrices and non-zero-centered disturbance sets for tight zonotopic uncertainty propagation. Our method, GPUSLS-LEO, enables online optimization of robust feedback policies that account for linearization error, producing tight, formally verified reachable tubes. On complex nonlinear and NN dynamics up to 168 state dimensions, our method can compute robust control policies on the GPU at rates up to 67 Hz, reducing solve times and conservativeness relative to baselines while preserving formal guarantees and real-time performance.

## I Introduction

Safe real-time nonlinear control under uncertainty is essential for the resilient operation of robots, drones, and spacecraft. This motivates methods for solving the robust nonlinear optimal control problem (RNOCP), which seeks a control policy that robustly guarantees constraint satisfaction under worst-case disturbances. In practice, RNOCP solvers typically optimize (1) a nominal trajectory and (2) a stabilizing feedback controller to track it under disturbance. Robust constraint satisfaction is enforced by tightening the nominal constraints using an overapproximation of the closed-loop tracking-error reachable tube, ensuring that the closed-loop dynamics remain in a safe subset of the state and input space. However, exact reachability via error propagation through nonlinear dynamics [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib1), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib2), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib3)] is generally intractable in real time. To address this, [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib5), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7)] approximate the nonlinear dynamics along a nominal trajectory with a linear time-varying (LTV) system and compute reachable sets using the LTV dynamics. System-level synthesis (SLS) [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib8), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)] is one such LTV robust control framework that can be solved in real time over long horizons for high-dimensional systems [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)].

Despite strong performance, LTV-based methods only guarantee robust constraint satisfaction given a bound on the linearization error, which captures the deviation between the true nonlinear dynamics and their LTV approximation. Existing methods often use global bounds [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11)], which yield conservative (loose) reachable tubes. Tighter local bounds around the nominal trajectory are often possible, but must be computed efficiently for real-time planning and informative enough to guide the optimizer toward safe trajectories with minimal linearization error. Thus, the challenge is to develop bounds that are simultaneously (1) tight, (2) real-time computable, and (3) differentiable, so an RNOCP solver can use them to reshape the nominal trajectory and tighten the reachable tubes. As existing methods do not achieve all three, many LTV-based RNOCP solvers must omit linearization error, forgoing formal guarantees for performance [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib12), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib13)].

To close this gap, we propose a family of tight, differentiable linearization error bounds (LEBs) for RNOCP solvers with nonlinear dynamics described by analytic functions and neural networks (NNs), with a GPU-parallel implementation in JAX. To make these LEBs compatible with the real-time SLS solver of [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9)], we extend the solver 1) to accommodate right-invertible disturbance matrices, enabling direct zonotopic propagation of the LEBs while avoiding the conservative overapproximations in [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib9)]; and 2) to handle disturbance sets that are not zero-centered. Finally, we show empirically that these bounds enable real-time, GPU-based computation of formally verified RNOCP solutions, with limited conservativeness for systems with up to 168 states and solve times as low as 15 ms. Our contributions are:

* • A set of tight, provably-sound linearization error bounding methods, including path-based interval bounds for analytic systems and NN verifier-based bounds for NN dynamics. * • A novel nonlinear SLS formulation that includes linearization error through tight zonotopic propagation, including treatment of right-invertible disturbance matrices and non-zero-centered disturbance sets, guaranteeing robust constraint satisfaction for the original nonlinear system. * • A GPU-accelerated nonlinear SLS solver, GPUSLS-LEO, that uses a formulation of these linearization bounds in JAX to enable differentiable, GPU-parallel evaluation and gradient-based robust nonlinear optimal control. * • Evaluation on analytic and NN dynamics models, maintaining real-time control rates (up to 67 Hz) for systems up to 168D and problems with ≈2×105\approx 2\times 10^{5} decision variables.

II Related Work
chunks.text:
## II Related Work

While linearization-free reachability methods exist [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib1), [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib2), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib3)], direct error propagation through nonlinear dynamics is generally intractable in real time, especially beyond ≈\approx10 states [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib3), [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib1)]. Thus, RNOCP solvers often rely on linearized error propagation for efficiency [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib14), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib13)], but introduce linearization error that is difficult to tightly bound, and is often ignored [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib14), [15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib15), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib13), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)], underapproximated via sampling [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)], or handled by assuming access to a linearization bound oracle [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib16), [17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib17), [18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib18), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib19), [20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib20)]. RNOCP solvers that explicitly compute LEBs typically rely on global Lipschitz estimates [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11)] or interval arithmetic [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7), [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib5), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib21)]. Interval arithmetic has been used both to compute reachable sets [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib22), [23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib23)] and to support reachability by constructing linear differential inclusion bounds (LDI) for nonlinear dynamics [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib24)]. In particular, [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib25)] uses Jacobian overbounding to obtain tighter LDIs for reachability, but is not used for control design or directly compute LEBs. Computationally, existing linearization bounding methods are offline [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)], slow, or non-differentiable [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7)], limiting their use for planning. To close these gaps, our method uses interval arithmetic and JAX to compute tight differentiable LEBs for direct use in optimal control. Moreover, we also adapt neural-network (NN) verification tools [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib26)] to derive affine bounds on linearization error for NN dynamics.

≈\approx

As LEBs can be slow to compute [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)], they are often generated once offline [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4), [11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib11)] but are loose if we wish to bound error around one trajectory, as in RMPC. Thus, practitioners often omit linearization error, yielding heuristic reachable tubes that trade formal guarantees for performance [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib12)]. To address this, we show that tight, local, GPU-parallel LEBs can be computed online while providing both real-time performance on high-dimensional systems and hard guarantees.

### VI-A Linearization Error

We compare the LEB from our path-based Hessian (PBH) method on the Satellite (nx=7n\_{x}=7, nu=3n\_{u}=3) and Quadrotor (nx=12n\_{x}=12, nu=4n\_{u}=4) systems (App. [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#A1 "Appendix A Dynamical System Definitions ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) with several baselines. Global sampling [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)] estimates worst-case curvature offline (taking over 7 minutes [[4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib4)]) over the *global* set 𝒳×𝒰\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}, yielding an empirical over-approximation. Interval Hessian (IH) (classic) [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib7)] evaluates ([12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S4.E12 "In IV-A Linearization Error Bounds for Analytic Dynamics ‣ IV GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")) on a local set 𝒯⊂(𝒳×𝒰)\mathcal{T}\subset(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}). IH (classic)-CORA denotes the standard IH implementation in CORA [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib6), [29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib29)]. Random sampling uses 10K samples from the local set and gives an *under-approximation*. We sample nominal points (z,v)(z,v) from 𝒳×𝒰\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U} and define local sets 𝒯:=(z,v)⊕ϵ​ℰnx+nu\mathcal{T}:=(z,v)\oplus\epsilon\mathcal{E}\_{n\_{x}+n\_{u}} with ϵ=0.01,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2\epsilon=0.01,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2. Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ VI-A Linearization Error ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") shows the mean interval width of ([23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S4.E23 "In IV-C Zonotope Bounds of ⁢ r k ( x k , u k , w k ) ‣ IV GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). For *Satellite*, where nonlinearity is mild, all over-approximation methods remain close to the random-sampling lower bound as ϵ\epsilon grows, though PBH is still the tightest. For *Quadrotor*, PBH consistently gives the tightest bounds. By contrast, global sampling is loose at small ϵ\epsilon, suggesting global curvature misses local behavior, while the interval Hessian becomes overly conservative at ϵ=0.20\epsilon=0.20. PBH runs in under 1 ms, enabling real-time use. Although slower than the global bound, which is efficiently calculated online after slow offline computation, PBH is 60% and 27% (satellite and quadrotor respectively) faster than dense random sampling and negligible running time compared to CORA IH.

### VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP

In this section, we evaluate GPUSLS-LEO on a suite of analytic and neural dynamical systems against various RNOCP baselines. #### VI-B4 Neural T-pusher

We demonstrate that our formulation can account for linearization error propagation through learned neural dynamics. We train an MLP-based model for the T-pusher system and task it with rotating and pushing the object to the goal configuration (Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")). We evaluate our method on several ablations (Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(a)), including GPUSLS, GSL (shorthand for GPUSLS-LEO), GSL-C (zero-centered zonotopes) and GSL (λ=1\lambda=1), which incorporates a penalty on the linearization error as defined in [V-B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S5.SS2 "V-B Efficient SLS Implementation on the GPU ‣ V Using Linearization Error Bounds in GPUSLS ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics"). Compared to GPUSLS, GPUSLS-LEO produces tubes that are on average 99% larger. However, Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(b) shows that our method achieves 100% containment of all rollouts, while Fig. [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B3 Coupled 3D Quadrotor ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics")(c) illustrates how trajectories from GPUSLS fall out of the tube, showing the need to formally consider linearization error.

#### VI-B5 Runtime

We evaluate the runtime of our method across all systems. In Tab. [III](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.T3 "TABLE III ‣ VI-B4 Neural T-pusher ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics"), we show the per iteration breakdown in milliseconds of the different components of our methodology. In all systems aside from the coupled quadrotor, the main computation load is in the GPUSLS, showing that our proposed modifications do not drastically increase run time. We also show that all total runtimes fall below the discretization time step DT, demonstrating the viability of our method under a real-time iteration MPC scheme [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)].

Finally, we evaluate the method’s scaling with growing state and control dimensions using an increasing number of coupled quadrotors. Fig. [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#S6.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B4 Neural T-pusher ‣ VI-B Using Linearization Bounds for RNOCP ‣ VI Results ‣ GPU-Parallel Linearization Error Bounds for Real-Time Robust Optimal Control of Nonlinear and Neural Network Dynamics") shows that GPUSLS incurs higher initial runtime but scales favorably with state and control dimension due to its logarithmic scaling [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2607.01203v1#bib.bib10)]. PBH on the other hand, exhibits low initial runtime, but can slow down in higher dimensions due to the cost of Hessian computations.
